mentions.author: maeon3
mentions.story: Sci-fi policing: L.A. police predicting crime before it occurs
mentions.text:
They don't say what methods they are employing to do this. I think I have a good idea.

A two layer neural network with input (features) as the profile of a crime in a certain city and all of the related circumstances reduced to numeric columns. That should be able to produce reliable predictions on where/when crimes happen.

Andrew Ng talks about how to build this two layer neural network here: [course]

Glue it together, feed it the data, refine the inputs, test the outputs and revise the inputs/features, and there you go.

And yes for the liberals, this is going to profile people on all of the politically incorrect data points, race, color, sex, orientation, drug use, etc.

mentions.author: webspiderus
mentions.story: Free online version of Stanford's Fall 2011 Intro to AI course
mentions.text:
I took a version of this class (also taught by Norvig and Thrun) last year, and I definitely found it very enjoyable. I ended up taking it after CS 229 (which covers the mathematical underpinnings of machine learning with some rigor), so I unfortunately couldn't evaluate how good of an introductory course to AI it would be (having covered a lot of the concepts prior), but even still it was a class I enjoyed. Of particular interest was hearing the instructors draw parallels to their work (particularly with Google and the DARPA challenge), which made a lot of the theoretical concepts much more tangible and helped me recognize their practical applications.
